newsitem.title: MEXICO: Violent protests soar in Mexico, study shows.
newsitem.headline: Violent protests soar in Mexico, study shows.

text.p: Violent protests in Mexico have soared this year with the sluggish economy remaining a wellspring of unrest and the impoverished South bearing the brunt of the troubles, a private sector study shows.

The study, conducted by Mexico's respected Group of Economists and Associates (GEA), showed that cases where conflicts turned violent almost tripled in the April-June period, compared with the same months in 1995.

That upward trend intensified in July and August after the emergence of a guerrilla army in southern Mexico in late June that carried out a coordinated assault on police and military posts in several states on Aug. 28.

The outbreaks of violence in a country racked last year by its worst economic crisis in half a century, ranged from overturning cars in political disputes to lynchings, riots, public beatings and deadly assaults by armed guerrillas.

"People are becoming ever more desperate. What you see is a whole resistance movement, people defending themselves from the crisis," said Guillermo Valdez, a GEA economist who has conducted the survey since President Ernesto Zedillo took office in December 1994.

"But in this huge mass of social protest, you don't see ... a unified movement for change. The protests are very disperse, very isolated. There is no organisation with the credibility to centralize their demands."

According to Valdez's survey, non-violent protests have fallen off from a peak in the second half of last year, when Mexico was plumbing the depths of recession. But cases where violence has broken out were on a sharp upswing.

The survey, compiled from reports in Mexican national newspapers, showed that social conflicts turned violent in 142 cases in the second quarter of 1996, up from 55 cases in the same period in 1995. In August alone, there were 56 cases.

In many cases, Valdez said, the fuse was lit when poor peasants, often of Indian race, sought land, justice or political rights in areas where the long-ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party, or PRI, was run by inflexible landowners.

Echoing the findings of the survey, a non-party commission mediating peace talks in the rebellious southern state of Chiapas warned on Friday about a growing climate of violence in Mexico, which it said could provoke state repression.
"One cannot conceal that the situation in the country is serious and it is pursuing a path toward violence and insecurity," the National Intermediation Commission said.

About a third of the incidents of unrest occurred in southern Mexican states such as Chiapas, Oaxaca and Guerrero, home bases of Mexico's two rebel armies, the survey showed. Another third are in and around the capital, suggesting the more prosperous north was spared the bulk of the trouble.
According to the study, of all social protests in the second quarter around 65 percent were of an economic nature, up from 40 percent in the previous quarter.
